subject: philosophy
title: Defend or criticize Socrates
objective: Interpret fairly, map the dispute, and answer an objection.

lesson.opening: This integrative challenge joins Apology and Crito. The objective questions test what follows from a reconstruction. The written work is self-reviewed for clarity, fidelity, and relevance; your stance is not an answer key.

sections.heading: An examined disagreement
sections.body:
You may defend or criticize the portrayed Socrates. Begin by stating an argument he is represented as offering. Distinguish its general principle from any disputed application, and keep a textual claim separate from a claim about the exact words of the historical speaker.

A criticism succeeds only if it addresses a reason the argument needs. A defense succeeds only if it answers the actual objection. Neither rhetorical confidence nor personal agreement substitutes for this work.

Your next step after this world is deeper work on Plato and, later, cross-tradition comparison. This MVP does not pretend those later lessons are already written. The challenge recognizes an initial ability to reconstruct a position, not permanent mastery of Socrates.

sections.heading: Reconstructing the argument
sections.body: The objection targets a premise needed to apply the principle. A defender should identify the grounds of the obligation and answer the challenge to them. A critic must not replace the argument with a blanket endorsement of every state command.

sections.heading: A serious objection
sections.body: A critic of the critic says civic cooperation would become unstable if everyone treated personal disagreement as release from obligation. The critic must address that institutional concern without conceding that every legal outcome is just.

activities.prompt: Which premise does the stated objection target?
choices: The application of a genuine obligation to this escape.
The claim that the dialogue has a title.
The claim that all questions have answers.

activities.prompt: Which is the fairest description of the source?
choices: An exact recording of every historical word.
Plato’s literary portrayal, which supports textual analysis and requires historical interpretation.

activities.prompt: Which comparison of Apology and Crito is careful?
choices: They straightforwardly prove unconditional state obedience.
The relation between civic duties and resistance to unjust commands needs interpretation.

activities.prompt: Which reply addresses the civic-stability objection?
choices: Give a public, principled account of when resistance is justified and why ordinary disagreement is insufficient.
Insult anyone who obeys a law.

activities.prompt: What does exposing inconsistent commitments establish by itself?
choices: At least one commitment needs revision or clarification.
The first claim is always the false one.

activities.prompt: What is the best evidence of understanding an argument you reject?
choices: You can reconstruct its reasons and locate the precise point of disagreement.
You agree with its author’s politics.

activities.prompt: Defend or criticize Socrates’ refusal to escape. First reconstruct the argument, then answer the strongest objection to your own view.
activities.context:
Reconstruction: Doing wrong is never justified merely by having suffered wrong. Escaping would violate a genuine obligation in this case. Therefore escape is not justified merely by the injustice suffered.
Objection: The second premise needs support. An unjust conviction may not create the obligation alleged.
rubric: My reconstruction is recognizable from the text.
I identify and defend or challenge a particular premise.
I answer an objection to my own position without grading by agreement.
